Le Crayon est le média du débat des 18-3: Le Crayon is the debate outlet for 18-35-year-olds, launched on YouTube in 2020. Behind it, siblings: Sixtine and Wallerand Moullé-Berteaux, who co-founded it with Antonin Marin and Jules Stimpfling. Sixtine had the idea in her final year of school; she co-founded the outlet at 19. Wallerand, now head of the group, is on the Forbes 30 Under 30 list. The YouTube channel has over 500,000 subscribers and 4,000 videos, and the outlet claims around three million followers across all platforms.
La forme : du débat sous toutes ses cout: The form: debate in every shape. Face-to-faces where a personality — politician, philosopher, creator — is questioned by young people, street interviews, debates between two young people who disagree on everything, in long formats for YouTube and short ones for TikTok and Instagram. The tone is very recognisable: frontal in the questions, calm in the exchange. It's one of the rare places on the internet where two people who disagree get to finish their sentence.
Réunir des gens qui ne pensent pas parei: Bringing together people who don't think alike and letting them follow their reasoning through. In the age of algorithms that reassure you, it has become rare.
Le Surligneur, agence de communication p: Le Surligneur, a communications agency for executives; Le Pinceau, a content agency for brands; Les Pépites de France, a tourism and heritage outlet bought by the group. Le Crayon is the heart of an ecosystem.
Le débat transpartisan et gratuit ne pai: Free, cross-party debate doesn't pay Paris rent; brands and executives do. Rather than sell their outlet, the founders built around it the means to fund it.
Le Crayon réussit ce que des médias cent: Le Crayon pulls off what outlets a hundred times richer have been failing at for ten years: making young people want to listen to each other disagree. And the business model is clever — the group's agencies fund the outlet's independence, where so many others have had to sell or subsidise it. The ambitions don't stop there: debates on stage, and even the idea of a physical venue entirely dedicated to the outlet.
Deux réserves et une demie. La neutralit: Two and a half reservations. The claimed neutrality is a permanent balancing act: when you give everyone a voice, each side accuses you of inviting the other. The second is more serious: housing under one roof an outlet, an agency advising executives and an agency producing for brands raises a real question of separation. We're not saying there's a problem; we're saying that the day the outlet interviews one of the agencies' clients, the wall will have to be very high. And the half: they're moving so fast this analysis may be out of date by the time you read it. To start, pick a face-to-face with a guest you don't like: if you last the twenty minutes, you've won.
